hints: If the stalls were in a straight line, you'd solve 'no two adjacent' with a simple DP. The circle only adds one extra rule — the first and last can't both be chosen. How can you remove that rule?

Run the straight-line DP twice: once on stalls 0..n−2 (skip the last) and once on stalls 1..n−1 (skip the first). The answer is the larger. Line DP: best = max(skip this stall, take it + best two back).

1. If n == 1 return coins[0].
  2. Define line(lo, hi): take = 0, skip = 0; for each stall, newTake = skip + coins[i], skip = max(skip, take), take = newTake; return max(take, skip).
  3. Return max(line(0, n−2), line(1, n−1)).

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every subset of stalls, keep those with no adjacent pair (circle-aware), take the best sum.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two runs of the linear 'no adjacent' DP, excluding the first or the last stall.

explain: For [2,7,9,3,1]: excluding the last stall, [2,7,9,3] gives best 2+9 = 11; excluding the first, [7,9,3,1] gives best 7+3 = 10 (or 9+1). Max is 11. Any valid choice in the circle either skips stall 0 or skips stall n−1, so the two runs together cover every case. For [3,4,3] the runs give 4 and 4, so the answer is 4. Handle n = 1 separately, since both ranges would be empty.
recognize: Pick non-adjacent items for max sum, and the items form a circle → run the linear house-robber DP twice, dropping the first or the last.
